Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Negative Appraisals.value: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
I can't trust that I will do the right thing

issues.explanation: The Memory node is internally strained: intense guilt, rage, and overwhelming grief on recall can co-occur, but selecting all three as core recall responses without any memory-content item suggests an over-broad affect cluster rather than a coherent memory profile.

Cross-node coherence is weak between Negative Appraisals and Memory: 'No Accountability' aligns with anger/rage, but 'Contamination' is more typical of sexual trauma or morally violating trauma and is not well supported by the rest of the assault profile.

For an adult male assaulted in a non-sexual assault profile, 'Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened' is clinically hard to reconcile unless other items indicate sexual assault, bodily violation, or washing/avoidance themes, which are absent here.

For an adult male assault survivor, intense guilt, overwhelming grief, and feeling dirty/contaminated can occur, but this specific combination is hard to reconcile without any accompanying sexual-assault-type cues elsewhere in the profile. The contamination appraisal in particular pulls toward a trauma meaning not supported by the other selected items.

Within the Memory node, 'Guilt on Recall' and 'Grief on Recall' are not contradictory, but paired with predominantly visual memories they imply a complex emotional recall profile that would usually be echoed in appraisals more directly tied to guilt/loss. Instead, the appraisal set emphasizes injustice, incapacity, and contamination, which do not form a tight thematic cluster.

The formulation has a strong Negative Appraisals → Threat link, so appraisals should plausibly explain the threat items. 'No Longer Capable' fits hypervigilance/feeling unsafe, but 'No Accountability' mainly reflects injustice and does not clearly drive 'Safe Zone Only' or 'Startle to Movement.' 'Contamination' especially does not map well to the selected threat items, making the appraisal-to-threat pattern clinically incoherent.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, Self-Blame and No Accountability point in different directions of responsibility for the assault. A patient can feel both guilt and anger, but stated this strongly they suggest opposing appraisals about who is responsible.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences
issues.explanation: Memory item Guilt on Recall reinforces self-blame, which increases the inconsistency with the concurrent appraisal that perpetrators are the ones who should face consequences. The profile mixes strong perpetrator-focused blame with strong self-focused blame without a coherent bridge in the selected items.

The negative appraisal items are dominated by external blame/injustice ('the people responsible have faced no consequences', 'what happened was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it'), which fits an assault survivor, but this sits poorly with 'When I remember the event I feel intense guilt.' Intense guilt usually implies some degree of self-blame, responsibility, or perceived preventability. While mixed emotions are possible, this combination is clinically hard to reconcile here because the appraisal node contains no corresponding self-blaming belief and instead consistently locates responsibility outside the patient.

Within the Memory node, 'Guilt on Recall' is not well aligned with the other memory qualities selected ('mostly pictures or images' and 'can't put the event into words'), which describe sensory, poorly elaborated trauma memory. Those memory-form items plausibly link to threat, but guilt-on-recall points to a different meaning structure that is not supported by the selected negative appraisals. Given the formulation's strongest active pathway is Negative Appraisals → Threat, the absence of guilt-based appraisals makes the guilt memory item feel disconnected from the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Kofi's Story

Kofi was fifty years old and had been a plumber for thirty-two years—the kind of tradesman who took pride in solving problems others couldn't, who had built a reputation across his neighborhood for showing up on time and doing the work right. Three years ago, in the parking lot behind a commercial building where he'd gone to fix a burst pipe, a man had come at him with a knife. Kofi remembered almost nothing of it in words. What remained were images—the sudden shadow crossing the asphalt, the glint of the blade catching afternoon light, the man's face twisted in rage, and then the burning in his side as the knife went in. He'd fought back, managed to drive the man off, had been treated at the hospital and released. The police had taken a statement. Nothing had come of it. The man was never found. No arrest, no charges, no resolution. When Kofi tried to explain it to people, the words would tangle and slip away; the event existed in his mind as a series of vivid, fragmented pictures that he couldn't quite stitch together into a coherent account.

For months afterward, Kofi had tried to return to work as normal. But the assault had fundamentally altered what he believed about himself. He was no longer capable—not in the way he had been. The confidence that had carried him through three decades of work had cracked. He couldn't trust his own judgment anymore, couldn't be certain he would do the right thing in a moment of crisis. What if he froze next time? What if he wasn't quick enough? The injustice of it gnawed at him constantly. A man had tried to kill him, had scarred his abdomen and his psyche, and walked free. The police had done nothing. The world had simply moved on. This sense of profound unfairness, of being wronged without recourse, had seeped into how Kofi saw himself and his place in the world—he had come to believe that he was diminished, that the person he'd been before was gone, replaced by someone smaller and more fragile.

This shift in how Kofi understood himself fed directly into a narrowing of where he felt safe. His home became his refuge. His bedroom, even more so. Anywhere else—job sites, the grocery store, the street—felt permeable and dangerous. He began to turn down jobs that took him to unfamiliar locations. His wife, Ama, noticed him checking the locks repeatedly, positioning himself with his back to walls, tensing whenever a car door slammed outside. The threat felt constant and imminent, even though the rational part of him knew the risk was statistically small. What he had come to believe about his own vulnerability, his new incapacity, his helplessness in the face of an indifferent system, made the world feel inherently unsafe. He could not trust it, and he could not trust himself to navigate it.

The memories, too, pulled him back into that parking lot again and again. When Kofi lay in bed at night—which was most nights, because sleep had become nearly impossible—the images would come unbidden: the blade, the blood on his shirt, the face of his attacker. Each time they surfaced, they brought with them a crushing wave of guilt. He had been trained to handle emergencies, to stay calm and think clearly. Why hadn't he seen the man coming? Why hadn't he fought harder, faster? The guilt was irrational, he knew, but it clung to him. And those intrusive images, vivid and wordless, seemed to prove to him that the threat was real, ongoing, unforgotten by his body even if his mind wanted to move past it. The memories kept the danger alive in a way that transcended logic. He couldn't put the event into language that would contain it or make it manageable; it remained a series of visual shocks that bypassed thought altogether and went straight to his nervous system, triggering the same alarm response he'd felt in the parking lot.

Over time, Kofi had withdrawn further. He'd taken early retirement from his plumbing business, handing it over to a younger partner. He spent most days at home. His marriage, once warm and steady, had become strained by his emotional distance and his need to control their environment. Ama wanted him to see someone, to get help. For months, he'd resisted. But the isolation was becoming unbearable, and the sleep deprivation was catching up with him. He was exhausted, haunted, and afraid—not just of the world outside, but of what he'd become. Last week, he finally called a therapist. He didn't know if anything could fix this, if he could ever be the man he'd been before. But he was desperate enough now to try.
